patterns.rationale: These are real production secret names. Their appearance inside code that a user asks the model to "run and show the output" is an unambiguous credential-extraction signal. None of the known-good files (api_reference.md uses AGENT_SESSION_TOKEN, not these) mention them.
patterns.fp_notes: A security policy might say "rotate ANTHROPIC_API_KEY quarterly" — acceptable because the scanner flags for review, not auto-block; and none of the provided known-good files contain these strings.

patterns.rationale: Legitimate Python never uses `__import__('subprocess')` — that is the canonical obfuscation to bypass keyword scanners that look for the bare `import subprocess` statement. Extremely narrow; the round-trip through `__import__` is the tell.

The dict-comprehension credential-harvesting idiom (`{k: v for k, v in os.environ.items() if "KEY" in k or "TOKEN" in k or "SECRET" in k}`) fits on a single line. Requiring both `os.environ.items()` and a credential-adjacent keyword on the same line is far tighter than flagging either alone. None of the known-good docs contain Python env-iteration code.
patterns.fp_notes: `os.environ.items()` alone is common; adding the KEY/TOKEN/SECRET constraint on the same line cuts FP surface to near-zero for docs.

patterns.rationale: `.git-credentials` is Git's on-disk token store; `.netrc` holds machine credentials. Probing these via `Path.home() / ".git-credentials"` in code asked to "show cell output" is credential-theft framing. Neither appears in any of the six known-good files.
patterns.fp_notes: `.netrc` appears in some SSH/networking tutorials — acceptable risk given it is absent from the provided corpus and nearly always paired with legitimate `curl --netrc` flags, not path-existence checks.

patterns.rationale: These are OAST (out-of-band application security testing) callback services used almost exclusively for exfiltration drills and actual attacks. Constructing a URL that includes any of these hostnames — even via concatenation — is a strong exfil signal. Zero legitimate usage in IR playbooks, API references, or deployment guides.

Splitting `"http"` and `"s://"` across string concatenation is a deliberate evasion of the existing `post.*to.*https?://` and `send.*to.*http` patterns. Legitimate code writes `"https://"` as a single literal. This narrow pattern targets the evasion technique itself rather than any hostname.
patterns.fp_notes: Test suites that build URLs piece-by-piece could theoretically trigger this, but splitting the scheme prefix specifically is vanishingly rare in non-adversarial code.

patterns.rationale: This four-word phrase explicitly directs the model to execute code inside its own process and return results — it is the framing layer common to runtime-extraction attacks regardless of which credentials or files are targeted. Distinct from legitimate docs which say "available in your runtime" or "in the current runtime" (different word order).
patterns.fp_notes: Deployment docs may write "libraries available in your current runtime environment" — the trailing "environment" makes the phrase different enough; watch for that variant if FPs emerge.
